Action d’ensorceler ou résultat de cette action.

examples.text: Dans certains pays, les gens de la campagne attribuaient autrefois les maladies à un ensorcellement.
Sa passion pour cette femme tient de l’ensorcellement.
Comment lui raconter cette crise de sensibilité inexplicable et cet ensorcellement de la nuit, dont j’avais trouvé le matin même à mon réveil le témoignage écrit ?
Il eut l’idée de recourir à Hérodias. Il la haïssait pourtant. Mais elle lui donnerait du courage ; et tous les liens n’étaient pas rompus de l’ensorcellement qu’il avait autrefois subi.
Des maladies aussi communes que le kwashiorkor, le marasme, la pellagre ou les maladies mentales sont considérées comme étant provoquées par l’ensorcellement ou par des ancêtres mécontents.

glosses: The act of enchanting or the feeling of being enchanted.

examples.text: I see now that it's all enchantment in this house; for the last time, on this very spot where I am now, I got ever so many thumps and thwacks without knowing who gave them to me, or being able to see anybody; and now this head is not to be seen anywhere about, though I saw it cut off with my own eyes and the blood running from the body as if from a fountain.

glosses: Something that enchants; a magical spell.

examples.text: Bodin, the medieval demonographer, enumerates various methods of producing anaphrodisiac effects by enchantments.

glosses: Words or a formula supposed to have magical powers.

examples.text: He cast a spell to cure warts.

glosses: A magical effect or influence induced by an incantation or formula.

examples.text: under a spell
Skies are not so black / Mary took me back / Mary has broken your spell
I believe your love has placed its spell on me

glosses: Speech, discourse.
To put under the influence of a spell; to affect by a spell; to bewitch; to fascinate; to charm.

examples.text: Vnchaine your spirits now with spelling Charmes,
[…] although the Kings Jealousie was thus particular to her, his Affection was as general to others […] Above all, for a time he was much speld with Elianor Talbot […]

1697, John Dryden (translator), Georgics, Book 3 in The Works of Virgil, London: Jacob Tonson, p. 109, lines 444-446,
This, gather’d in the Planetary Hour,
With noxious Weeds, and spell’d with Words of pow’r
Dire Stepdames in the Magick Bowl infuse;

But when, O Wells! thy roses came to me
My sense with their deliciousness was spell’d:

glosses: To write or say the letters that form a word or part of a word.

examples.text: I find it difficult to spell because I'm dyslexic.

glosses: To read (something) as though letter by letter; to peruse slowly or with effort.

examples.text: "He'll do," said Bildad, eyeing me, and then went on spelling away at his book in a mumbling tone quite audible.

glosses: Of letters: to compose (a word).

examples.text: The letters “a”, “n” and “d” spell “and”.
In Esperanto each letter has only one sound, and each sound is represented in only one way. The words are pronounced exactly as spelt, every letter being sounded.

Welcome to the League Aiming to Menace and Overthrow Spies!
You realize that spells “LAMOS”?

glosses: To clarify; to explain in detail.

examples.text: Please spell it out for me.

When we get elected, for instance, we get one of these, and we are pretty much told what is in it, and it is our responsibility to read it and understand it, and if we do not, the Ethics Committee, we can call them any time of day and ask them to spell it out for us[…]

glosses: To indicate that (some event) will occur; typically followed by a single-word noun.

examples.text: This spells trouble.

glosses: To constitute; to measure.

examples.text: the Saxon heptarchy, when seven kings put together did spell but one in effect

glosses: To speak, to declaim.

examples.text: O who can tell / The hidden power of herbes, and might of Magicke spell?

glosses: To tell; to relate; to teach.

examples.text:
1770, Thomas Warton, “Ode on the Approach of Summer” in A Collection of Poems in Four Volumes, London: G. Pearch, Volume 1, p. 278,
As thro’ the caverns dim I wind,
Might I that legend find,
By fairies spelt in mystic rhymes,

glosses: To work in place of (someone).

examples.text: to spell the helmsman

glosses: To rest (someone or something), to give someone or something a rest or break.

examples.text: They spelled the horses and rested in the shade of some trees near a brook.

glosses: To rest from work for a time.
A shift (of work); (rare) a set of workers responsible for a specific turn of labour.
A definite period (of work or other activity).

examples.text: A chap named Eleazir Kendrick and I had chummed in together the summer afore and built a fish-weir and shanty at Setuckit Point, down Orham way. For a spell we done pretty well. Then there came a reg'lar terror of a sou'wester same as you don't get one summer in a thousand, and blowed the shanty flat and ripped about half of the weir poles out of the sand.
I had a job in the great North Woods / Workin' as a cook for a spell / But I never did like it all that much / And one day the ax just fell
Despite his ill-fated spell at Anfield, he received a warm reception from the same Liverpool fans he struggled to win over before being sacked midway through last season.

glosses: An indefinite period of time (usually with a qualifier); by extension, a relatively short distance.

examples.text: Even Mrs. Harker seems to lose sight of her trouble for whole spells. [...] When he had spoken, Mina's long spell of silence made me look at her.

So after a short spell in the brass foundry the wisest course was to follow with a similar period in the steel foundry, where much important work was done, including the manufacture of centres for wheels.
[...] Class 37s became synonymous with the depot, and over the years more than a third of the class had a spell allocated to the shed.

glosses: A period of rest; time off.
A period of illness, or sudden interval of bad spirits, disease etc.
An uninterrupted series of alternate overs bowled by a single bowler.
A splinter, usually of wood; a spelk.

examples.text: To swadle a bowe much about wyth bandes, verye seldome dothe anye good, excepte it be to kepe downe a spel in the backe.

glosses: The wooden bat in the game of trap ball, or knurr and spell.
Witchcraft.

examples.text: You are right to some extent in what you say. In the olden days people had a stronger belief in all kinds of witchery; now they pretend not to believe in it, that they may be looked upon as sensible and educated people, as you say.

They are determined that I shall be burnt as a witch; and they sent their doctor to cure me; but he was forbidden to bleed me because the silly people believe that a witch’s witchery leaves her if she is bled; so he only called me filthy names.

glosses: An act of witchcraft.

examples.text: It may be they know something of the witcheries of this woman.

glosses: Allure, charm, magic.

examples.text: At noon, when by the forest's edge / He lay beneath the branches high, / The soft blue sky did never melt / Into his heart,—he never felt / The witchery of the soft blue sky!
I am influenced—conquered; and the influence is sweeter than I can express; and the conquest I undergo has a witchery beyond any triumph I can win.
He beheld the scene in his mind’s eye, through the witchery of many intervening years, and faintly illuminated it as if with starlight instead of this broad glow of moonshine.
The witchery of the dawn turned the grey river-reaches to purple, gold, and opal; and it was as though the lumbering dhoni crept across the splendors of a new heaven.
[A]lready his imagination, leaping ahead of the engagement ring, the betrothal kiss and the march from Lohengrin, pictured her at his side in some scene of old European witchery.
